pr_title: pkg/kubelet: add KUBE-FIREWALL-IN chain, move localnet rule to it
pr_body:
@champtar observed that the rule added in #91569 still allowed packets through unidirectionally, meaning UDP with a spoofed source wouldn't be caught. So we need to filter on source interface.

However, KUBE-FIREWALL is run on both OUTPUT and INPUT, so it can't reference interfaces. This PR, thus,
- creates a chain KUBE-FIREWALL-IN
- Add it to INPUT, pass through to KUBE-FIREWALL
- Move the localnet protection rule to KUBE-FIREWALL-IN, and adjust it
  to reference source if, not source address.

Signed-off-by: Casey Callendrello <cdc@redhat.com>


**What type of PR is this?**
/kind bug

**What this PR does / why we need it**:

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:
Fixes #90259

**Special notes for your reviewer**:
You can test this pretty simply using `cnitool` if you don't want to spin up a whole kind cluster.


**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**:
```release-note
NONE
```

/sig network

@squeed good catch, I only tested that `127.0.0.1:NodePort` was working, nothing more ...
In that case you need a KUBE-FIREWALL-IN and KUBE-FIREWALL-OUT that chain to KUBE-FIREWALL
Created KUBE-FIREWALL-IN, but not KUBE-FIREWALL-OUT, since we don't need it (yet). If this should exist for symmetry, I'm happy to add it.
/hold cancel
/cc @danwinship
/retest

well, this is ugly.
we put this into the `KUBE-FIREWALL` chain before because it seemed to logically make sense, but given that that won't work, would it be better to just create a new chain (`KUBE-SECURITY`?) only for input, rather than doing the nested thing?

> would it be better to just create a new chain?

Do we have any sort of "API guarantees" around the existence of certain chains? Are users expecting to be able to add rules to KUBE-FIREWALL?

If not, then we should just move to KUBE-FIREWALL-IN and KUBE-FIREWALL-OUT and be done with it.

@danwinship the nesting is not mandatory, we can add both to INPUT
```
INPUT
-j KUBE-FIREWALL
-j KUBE-FIREWALL-IN
```
Our iptables chains are not _supposed_ to be API, but we don't know whether people depend on them. But I meant something like what @champtar said, though with a different name than `KUBE-FIREWALL-IN`

I specifically named it KUBE-FIREWALL-IN to indicate it's only for INPUT and thus can predicate on incoming interface `-i lo`. Naming it `KUBE-SECURITY` misses this context.

Annoyingly, iptables happily lets you shoot yourself in the foot; you can't do ` iptables -A OUTPUT -i lo ...`, but you can jump to a chain from OUTPUT that does.

Given that this is getting a bit uglier, I can also try and move this to the proxy code (iptables & ipvs), since they're the ones setting the offending sysctl anyways.
/uncc

Hey @champtar, I'm not sure this is necessary. The packets you observed (spoofed source IP of 127.0.0.2) will be blocked by the reverse path filter. Unless, of course, that's also disabled.

Given that disabling rpf is not so common on kubernetes nodes, I think we can just close this.

So @squeed you are right it seems we need `rp_filter=0` to be vulnerable

Hi,

The original iptables rule caused our cluster tests to fail on `kubectl exec`. The kubelet connected to the local privileged port with the node ip as the source, thus matching the conditions (`src != 127.0.0.1/8, dst = 127.0.0.1/8`)

Errors looked like this
```
# kubectl --namespace k8s exec k8s-dns-d584d5d8c-tk5bt -- echo it works
error: unable to upgrade connection: error dialing backend: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:36827: connect: connection timed out
```

After removing the firewall from OUTPUT :see_no_evil: and changing the rule I can exec again into pods
```
# iptables -R KUBE-FIREWALL 2 -m comment --comment "block incoming localnet connections" --dst 127.0.0.1/8 \! -i lo -m conntrack \! --ctstate RELATED,ESTABLISHED,DNAT -j DROP
# iptables -F OUTPUT
```
```
kubectl --namespace k8s exec k8s-dns-d584d5d8c-tk5bt -- echo it works
it works
```

This is currently blocking recent kubernetes version for us. Please cherry-pick onto 1.18 once merged.

issue_context.title: net.ipv4.conf.all.route_localnet=1 opens security issue
issue_context.body:
**What happened**:

`net.ipv4.conf.all.route_localnet=1` is set by `kube-proxy` in both iptables and ipvs mode. This causes a security issue;

A host on the local segment can actually route 127.0.0.1 to a k8s-node and access ports that really should be local.

Linux doc;
```
route_localnet - BOOLEAN
        Do not consider loopback addresses as martian source or destination
        while routing. This enables the use of 127/8 for local routing purposes.
        default FALSE
```

**What you expected to happen**:

Make `net.ipv4.conf.all.route_localnet=1` configurable and set only when needed.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

On a machine on the same network segment as the k8s nodes;
```
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.route_localnet=1
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians=1
#ip addr del 127.0.0.1/32 dev lo (does not work)
ip ro del 127.0.0.1/32 table local
ip ro add 127.0.0.1/32 via 192.168.1.2
tcpdump -ni eth1 port 10248  # In a separate shell
telnet 127.0.0.1 10248
```
The example uses port `10248` which is opened by kubelet on 127.0.0.1 only;
```
$ netstat -putln | grep 10248
tcp        0      0 127.0.0.1:10248         0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      252/kubelet         
```
I really can't the the connect working myself on plain linux with the instruction above. I got this info from others who claim they can. What I do see though is that the syn-ack is sent back, so I guess some spy program can exploit this;
```
10:42:45.451542 IP 192.168.1.201.42696 > 127.0.0.1.10248: Flags [S], seq 2493074034, win 64240, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 1895499143 ecr 0,nop,wscale 6], length 0
10:42:45.452539 IP 127.0.0.1.10248 > 192.168.1.201.42696: Flags [S.], seq 1282952108, ack 2493074035, win 65160, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 385731535 ecr 1895483715,nop,wscale 7], length 0
```
If you set net.ipv4.conf.all.route_localnet=0 manually on the target node the syn-acks will not be sent back;
```
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.route_localnet=0
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians=1
tail /var/log/messages
Apr 18 10:54:22 (none) user.warn kernel: IPv4: martian destination 127.0.0.1 from 192.168.1.201, dev eth1
Apr 18 10:54:23 (none) user.warn kernel: IPv4: martian destination 127.0.0.1 from 192.168.1.201, dev eth1
```


**Anything else we need to know?**:

Related issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/90236

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
  `v1.19.0-alpha.1.547+250884c9c1cd41`
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: Kvms on Ubuntu
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`): [xcluster](https://github.com/Nordix/xcluster)
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): `Linux 5.4.2 #2 SMP Thu Apr 16 17:58:35 CEST 2020`
- Install tools: "from scratch"
- Network plugin and version (if this is a network-related bug): (any)
- Others:
comments: /sig network

> This allows some corner cases of `-j DNAT` in iptables, but honestly I forget the details.

The case is connecting to `127.0.0.1:$NODEPORT`. Let's say that's 8888, pointing to pod 10.0.0.1:9999.

1. Emit packet. `127.0.0.1:xxxxx -> 127.0.0.1:8888`
2. NAT PREROUTING rules run, do DNAT, add conntrack entry. packet is `127.0.0.1:xxxxx -> 10.0.0.1:9999`
3. Routing decision. normally, 127.0.0.1 would be dropped as a martian, but `route_localnet` permits this. The outgoing interface is decided.
4. NAT POSTROUTING rules run, do MASQ, add conntrack entry. packet is now `$HostIP:xxxx -> 10.0.0.1:9999`

This sets up the conntrack entries for the packet to flow back from the pod to the tcp socket on localhost. You need to get the packet past the martian barrier, though, for this to work.
